messages.subject: Error message
parts:
Bob,

The error message is fairly clear to me, and I think the information needs to be preserved for the user, even if not printed immediately.

If you can eliminate the first part (the warning that an error is coming) and the second part (the error) entirely, I'd say it would be good to have three counters in STAN: one in which iteration the error first occurs, one in which iteration the error last occurs, and one that counts how many times the error occurred. Then, at the end of a run, print a warning that lists these three counters. and refers the user to some pithy advice in the manual. (Maybe something like, "If the error occurs once and it is on the first iteration, you're probably okay, but should check the constraints of your parameters, looking for boundary conditions like lower=0 when the parameter should be strictly greater than zero. If the error occurs more than once, this is a sign of instability in ...")

Speaking of which, I notice that in various examples in the manual, you use <lower=0> when it appears that the value should be strictly greater than zero. I usually put <lower=0.001> in such situations. Is this correct, or am I confused?


On Jul 10, 2013, at 1:49 PM, stan-...@googlegroups.com wrote:
    We put that message in for diagnostic reasons and it's been confusing
    users ever since.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error message
parts:
On 7/10/13 5:55 PM, Wayne Folta wrote:
> Bob,
>
> The error message is fairly clear to me, and I think the information needs to be preserved for the user, even if not
> printed immediately.
>
> If you can eliminate the first part (the warning that an error is coming) and the second part (the error) entirely, I'd
> say it would be good to have three counters in STAN: one in which iteration the error first occurs, one in which
> iteration the error last occurs, and one that counts how many times the error occurred. Then, at the end of a run, print
> a warning that lists these three counters. and refers the user to some pithy advice in the manual.

This would be very hard to build into the interface
without really cluttering things up for handling this
particular message. I'd rather just print it every
iteration as we do.

The embedded "error" is the message thrown by the
distribution code that's called. That really shouldn't
change, either. We want to print it. It should probably
say "exception", but that seems awfully programming-language
oriented to report back to a user.

> (Maybe something
> like, "If the error occurs once and it is on the first iteration, you're probably okay, but should check the constraints
> of your parameters, looking for boundary conditions like lower=0 when the parameter should be strictly greater than
> zero. If the error occurs more than once, this is a sign of instability in ...")

> Speaking of which, I notice that in various examples in the manual, you use <lower=0> when it appears that the value
> should be strictly greater than zero. I usually put <lower=0.001> in such situations. Is this correct, or am I confused?

If you have

real<lower=0> sigma;

then the lower=0 is theoretically an exclusive lower bound and the
constrained variable should be in the open interval (0,+infinity).

In this case, if the unconstrained parameter is sigma_raw, then
sigma = exp(sigma_raw). Now exp() always returns a positive value
in theory. Unlike for real numbers, in double-precision floating
point, if sigma_raw < -800 or so, exp(sigma_raw) will underflow and return 0.
It'll overflow to +infinity if sigma_raw > 800 or so. (+infinity is
a valid floating point value in C++ and hence in Stan.

We've also extended some of the distributions to deal with
boundaries of 0 or +infinity or -infinity. That part of the
code could stand to be cleaned up in terms of tests and
making sure all the boundary behaviors are as general as possible.

- Bob
